readerTitle: Your customers already wrote your best headline
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 서비스, 신발 가게) · 실제 기업·수치 없음
insight: 좋은 문구는 새로 지어내는 것이 아니라, 고객이 이미 하고 있는 말에서 찾아 옮겨 적는 것이다.
misconception: 전문가답고 세련된 말로 써야 신뢰를 얻는다. 고객의 평범한 말은 문구로 쓰기엔 너무 소박하다.

sources.text: 카피라이팅 실무의 일반 원칙 ('voice of customer' 조사: 리뷰, 문의, 상담 기록에서 고객 표현 수집)
모든 사례는 설명용 가상 예시이며 통계나 연구 수치를 인용하지 않음

factChecks.note: 레슨에 통계, 연구 결과, 실제 기업 사례가 없습니다. 모든 장면과 문구는 가상입니다. 검토 시 수치가 새로 들어가지 않았는지 확인하세요.
7번 카드의 '고객 이름이나 리뷰를 그대로 인용하기 전에 허락을 구하라'는 일반적인 예의 수준의 조언입니다. 특정 국가의 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Your customers already wrote your best headline
body: A house-cleaning company prints a flyer: *Professional residential sanitation services.*
The phone rings. The caller says, "I'm just tired of spending every Saturday cleaning." The next caller says almost the same thing. Nobody has ever asked for *residential sanitation*.

image.label: A formal cleaning flyer beside a phone showing a casual customer message
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 왼쪽에 딱딱한 전단지("Professional residential sanitation services"), 오른쪽에 스마트폰 화면의 고객 메시지 말풍선("I'm tired of spending every Saturday cleaning"). 두 문구의 온도 차이가 보이게. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Pick the new flyer headline.
body: You run that cleaning business. When people book, they often mention their weekends, coming home tired, or never catching up.
Which headline should lead the new flyer?

options.text: Professional home cleaning. Fully insured, eco-friendly products.
options.feedback: Clear and reassuring, so it helps. But it describes what you do in your words, not the moment the customer is living.

options.text: Come home to a clean house. Keep your Saturday.
options.feedback: It repeats what callers already say, so readers recognize their own thought. You give up sounding grand, and gain sounding like them.

options.text: Sparkle Squad: where clean meets care
options.feedback: Memorable, maybe. But a busy reader has to decode it, and it says nothing about the problem they called with.

cards.title: The words were sitting in her inbox.
body: The owner reads back through her reviews and booking messages. The same phrases keep coming up: "my weekend back," "come home to," "finally caught up."
Not one message says *sanitation*, *residential* or *solutions*. Those words came from her, not from her customers.
She had been writing in the language of the job. Her customers were speaking the language of their lives.

cards.title: The customer's own words
body: Using **the customer's own words** means building your message from the exact phrases customers use to describe their problem and the result they want.
It works because people notice what they recognize. When a sign says what you were already thinking, it feels written for you. Customers also search and scan using their own vocabulary, not yours.

image.label: Phrases lifted from reviews and dropped into a headline
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 리뷰·문자·통화 메모 카드들이 흩어져 있고, 그중 반복되는 문구("my weekend back", "come home to")에 형광펜 표시. 화살표로 오른쪽 헤드라인에 그대로 옮겨지는 모습.

cards.title: Where to find the words.
body: You don't need a survey. The words already exist in places most businesses ignore.
list: **Reviews:** yours and your rivals', especially the 3- and 4-star ones
**First messages:** how people describe the problem when they first get in touch
**Questions before buying:** what they worry about
**Reasons for leaving:** what they say when they cancel or don't return
cards.callout: Copy the phrase itself, not your summary of it.

cards.title: Experts name the fix. Customers name the pain.
body: A plumber thinks *hydro-jetting*. The customer types "kitchen drain keeps clogging." An accountant offers *bookkeeping reconciliation*. The client says "I never know how much money I actually have."
The more expert you are, the wider this gap tends to be. Your training gives you precise words that customers never use.
cards.softwareNote: Software teams write "workflow automation." Users write "I'm sick of copying data between spreadsheets." Support tickets and cancellation notes are often the best headline drafts a product team owns.

cards.title: Listen for patterns, not one loud voice.
body: One vivid quote can mislead you. Use a phrase only when many customers say something similar. Different groups may also use different words, so check whose words you're borrowing.
Customers describe problems well, but they may not know your product's name for the fix. Use their words for the pain and plain words for the solution.
And ask before quoting a customer by name.

cards.title: Now it's a shoe shop.
body: You stock shoes with wide toes and thick cushioning. The supplier's tag says *orthotic comfort technology*. Nurses, cooks and shop workers keep asking, "Do you have anything for standing all day?"
What should the shelf sign say?

options.feedback: Accurate, but it's the supplier's language. Shoppers walking past won't connect it to their sore feet.

options.text: On your feet all day? Start here.
options.feedback: It echoes the question shoppers already ask, so the right people stop. You trade technical detail for instant recognition; staff can explain the rest.
Clear, which beats clever. But every shoe claims comfort, and it misses the specific situation customers keep describing.

cards.title: Write down what customers say before you write what you sell.
body: Your best message is often a phrase a customer has already said many times. Your job is to notice it and repeat it.
**Try it today:** read your last ten reviews or customer messages. Underline any phrase that appears more than once. Compare it with your current headline.
